content: People living with advanced HIV disease are at a significantly increased risk of severe bacterial infections, including bloodstream infections, respiratory infections, central nervous system infections, and gastrointestinal infections. These infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in this population. However, the true burden of these infections is poorly characterized due to the lack of adequate diagnostic facilities in many settings. It is estimated that severe bacterial infections account for more than one-third of hospitalizations among adults and children living with HIV worldwide. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) offers protection against some, but not all, severe bacterial infections. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends lifelong co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for all individuals living with HIV in regions where severe bacterial infections or malaria are highly prevalent, regardless of CD4 cell count. However, increasing antimicrobial resistance complicates the treatment of severe bacterial infections in this population. Cryptococcal meningitis remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality among people living with HIV, despite the widespread availability of antiretroviral therapy (ART). A 2014 review estimated 223,100 new cases of cryptococcal meningitis globally, with 73% of cases occurring in sub-Saharan Africa. The annual global deaths from cryptococcal meningitis were estimated at 181,100. Cryptococcal meningitis is a leading cause of death among hospitalized adults living with HIV, accounting for 15–20% of adult deaths, though it is less common among children living with HIV. WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of cryptococcal meningitis, including pre-emptive therapy for asymptomatic individuals who test positive for cryptococcal antigen. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) is another leading cause of mortality among hospitalized adults (13%) and children (29%) living with HIV. However, the global burden of PJP-related morbidity and mortality is poorly understood due to the lack of diagnostic facilities in many settings. This highlights the need for improved diagnostic approaches and better access to co-trimoxazole and ART. Cerebral toxoplasmosis is the most common cause of expansive brain lesions among adults living with HIV who are not receiving co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. Toxoplasmosis is a common protozoan infection in people with HIV, with high prevalence rates in sub-Saharan Africa (45%), Latin America and the Caribbean (49%), and North Africa and the Middle East (61%). Individuals with latent toxoplasmosis are at risk of developing cerebral toxoplasmosis when their CD4 count falls below 200 cells/mm³. Diagnosis of cerebral toxoplasmosis requires imaging techniques, such as CT scans, which are often unavailable in resource-limited settings. Approximately 15% of hospitalized adults living with HIV who die from AIDS-related illnesses succumb to cerebral toxoplasmosis. Treatment options include high-dose co-trimoxazole or pyrimethamine-based regimens, which are equally effective, though co-trimoxazole is more readily available in resource-limited settings. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is a systemic viral infection that commonly manifests as CMV retinitis in severely immunocompromised individuals. The prevalence of CMV retinitis is highest in Asia and lower in Africa. Among children, CMV is responsible for CMV pneumonitis, and HIV-exposed infants have a higher incidence of congenital CMV infection. Other fungal infections, such as histoplasmosis and talaromycosis, are associated with advanced HIV disease in specific geographic regions. Histoplasmosis is particularly prevalent in Central and South America, where it is a leading cause of AIDS-related deaths. The lack of simple diagnostic tests limits knowledge of the disease burden. Amphotericin B has been shown to improve clinical outcomes in talaromycosis and should be made available to people living with HIV who have this infection. The WHO 2016 consolidated antiretroviral guidelines recommend starting ART regardless of CD4 cell count. However, baseline CD4 cell count testing remains critical for identifying individuals with advanced HIV disease who may require additional care interventions. Clinical staging alone is insufficient, as many individuals with severe immune suppression may be misclassified. CD4 cell count testing is also valuable for guiding clinical management in cases of virological treatment failure. A package of care interventions, including screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and intensified adherence support, should be offered to all individuals presenting with advanced HIV disease. This package includes co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, TB preventive treatment, cryptococcal antigen screening, and pre-emptive antifungal therapy for those with positive cryptococcal antigen results. Enhanced adherence support is particularly beneficial for individuals with advanced HIV disease, especially during acute illness and the immediate post-discharge period. Two randomized trials, REMSTART and REALITY, have demonstrated the effectiveness of targeted intervention packages in reducing mortality and morbidity among people with advanced HIV disease. The REMSTART trial, conducted in Tanzania and Zambia, showed a 28% reduction in mortality with a combination of community support, cryptococcal antigen screening, and pre-emptive antifungal treatment. The REALITY trial, conducted in Kenya, Malawi, Uganda, and Zimbabwe, demonstrated reductions in TB incidence (28%), cryptococcal disease (62%), and hospitalizations (17%) with an enhanced prophylaxis package. These findings highlight the importance of early prophylaxis and comprehensive care for individuals with advanced HIV disease. Despite these advances, concerns remain about the routine use of certain interventions, such as broad-spectrum antibiotics and primary fluconazole prophylaxis, due to potential antimicrobial resistance, cost, and safety concerns. Further research is needed to assess the role of these interventions in reducing mortality from severe bacterial infections and cryptococcal disease.
